title: Hungary’s 1949 election had one list, and an unmarked ballot counted as a yes
body: After the war Hungary held a fairly free election: on 4 November 1945 the Smallholders won 57% and the Communists 17%. Then the Communist leader Mátyás Rákosi split, banned and jailed his rivals one slice at a time (the “salami tactics”), and on 12 June 1948 the Social Democrats were merged into his party as the Hungarian Working People’s Party (MDP). On 15 May 1949 voters got a **single list**, the People’s Front’s, drawn up by the MDP. A yes needed no mark: the ballot went in as it was; a no meant crossing out a circle with two lines, and a polling committee could note who lingered in the booth. The Interior Ministry counted 95.6% of those who voted for the list ([György Gyarmati, Betekintő](https://www.betekinto.hu/sites/default/files/betekinto-szamok/2015_2_gyarmati.pdf)). On 20 August 1949 a constitution on the Soviet model of 1936 made Hungary a People’s Republic. Around Rákosi grew a cult copied from Stalin’s: for his 60th birthday, on 9 March 1952, gifts from all over the country filled the former Palace of Justice in Budapest ([Museum of Ethnography](https://neprajz.hu/en/kiallitasok/idoszaki/2012eng/rakosi60-at-neprajz.hu.html)).

slides.question: In Hungary’s single-list election of 15 May 1949, what share of those who voted backed the list, by the official count?
slides.explanation: 95.6% by the Interior Ministry’s count: 5,478,515 of 5,730,519 ballots. 165,283 voted against, 86,721 ballots were invalid, and 323,273 people on the roll did not vote.

slides.alt: Animation on a dark red poster background: the 1945 election as bars, rival parties sliced away, two parties merging into the MDP, a one-list ballot dropped into a box or crossed out, the official 95.6% bar, a Soviet-model constitution, and gilt frames for Stalin and Rákosi.

slides.prompt: Try all four things a voter could do with the 1949 ballot: what could the polling committee see?
slides.takeaway: Only a yes took no act at all: 5,478,515 dropped the ballot in as it was, 95.6% of those who voted and 90.5% of everyone on the roll. A no took two strokes behind the curtain.

left.label: 4 November 1945
left.text: Several parties and a secret ballot: Smallholders 57%, Social Democrats 17%, Communists 17%.

right.label: 15 May 1949
right.text: One list, drawn up by the Communist-led MDP. A yes needed no mark at all: 95.6% for the list.

events.text: A constitution on the Soviet model

slides.question: In Hungary’s single-list election of 1949, what did a voter have to do to vote against the list?
options: Cross out a circle with two lines
slides.explanation: An unmarked ballot counted as a yes. A no meant crossing out the circle with two lines, behind the curtain, where taking long could be noted.

source.label: Betekintő: György Gyarmati on Hungary’s election of 1949 (in Hungarian)
